# How to Draft a Polite Follow-up Email After a Job Interview

> **In short:** Send a short, specific thank-you email within 24 hours of the interview — three or four sentences, one fresh detail from the chat, and a clear next step. Keep it warm, not needy; this guide shows you exactly what to write and what to avoid.

A good follow-up email is one of the few small things still fully in your control after an interview. It takes about ten minutes to write, and it quietly reminds the hiring manager who you are. Below is a simple, friendly process you can follow the same day, even if you've just walked out of the meeting room still buzzing.

## Before you start
- **Time needed:** roughly 10–15 minutes, ideally within 24 hours of the interview.
- **What you need:** the interviewer's name, their email address, and the job title you applied for. A notes app (your phone is fine) where you scribbled two or three things that came up in the conversation.
- **Tool:** any email app or webmail — Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail, whatever you already use. No special software required.
- **Optional:** an AI assistant (such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude) can help you polish your draft, but it cannot send the email for you, and it doesn't know what was actually said in the interview — that's your job to feed in.

## Step 1 — Jot down three things you actually talked about
Open your notes app the moment you can after the interview — even two minutes in the car park is better than waiting. Write down three specific things that came up: a question they asked, a story you told, a detail about the role or the team. These are the bricks you'll build the email from. **What you see:** your phone's notes app, the date at the top, and probably a few messy half-sentences. **What happens next:** you'll have raw material to pull from, so the email can sound like *you* and not like a template you copied off the internet. **If it looks different:** if you didn't take notes, try to recall one question you were asked and one thing you said that landed well. Even one believable detail is enough. **You'll know it worked when** you have at least two concrete points you can reference in the email — something the interviewer would recognise as "ours, not just any interview."
💬 Example: *Asked about handling an angry customer → I told the café story. Mentioned the new Brisbane office opens in March.*

## Step 2 — Open a new email and set the subject line
Open your email app and click **Compose** (or **New Message**). For the subject line, keep it short and easy to scan — the interviewer gets a lot of mail. A clear subject line is like a polite wave from across a crowded room: it says "this is the person you met today, not a stranger." **What you see:** a blank email with a To, Subject and message area. **What happens next:** the moment you type their name correctly, the email already feels more personal than half the inbox they'll skim today. **If it looks different:** on some apps the button says **New email**, **Write**, or shows a pencil icon — any of these will do. **You'll know it worked when** the subject clearly says thank-you, names the role, and is short enough to read fully on a phone screen.
💬 Example: `Subject: Thank you — Marketing Coordinator interview`

## Step 3 — Open with a warm, specific thank-you
In the first one or two sentences, thank the interviewer by name and mention something specific from your conversation. This is the part that turns a generic "thanks for the interview" into a real, human note. **What you see:** the cursor blinking at the top of the message body. **What happens next:** the reader instantly knows this email is about them and the meeting they actually had — not a copy-paste sent to ten companies. **If it looks different:** if you interviewed with a panel, address the lead person by name and use "and the team" for the rest. **You'll know it worked when** the first paragraph would only make sense to someone who was in that room.
💬 Example: *Hi Sarah, thank you so much for taking the time to chat with me this morning about the Marketing Coordinator role. I really enjoyed hearing how the team is planning the March launch.*

## Step 4 — Briefly reinforce why you're a fit
Now add two or three sentences that gently remind them of your strengths, tied to something you actually discussed. This is where your notes from Step 1 come in. Think of it like adding one fresh photo to a friend's birthday card — small, but it shows you remembered. **What you see:** the email is taking shape — it's getting longer than a text but shorter than a letter. **What happens next:** the interviewer gets a quick, evidence-based recap of why you belong in the role, without you having to repeat your whole CV. **If it looks different:** if the conversation was mostly about the company or the role itself, you can skip this part and go straight to Step 5 — a thoughtful question can carry the same weight. **You'll know it worked when** the reader can see, in plain words, that you understood the role and can do it.
💬 Example: *Our chat about managing the café's social media during the weekend rush reminded me how much I enjoy fast-paced, customer-facing work — that's exactly the energy I'd love to bring to your team.*

## Step 5 — Close with a clear, low-pressure next step
End with one short sentence that says you're looking forward to hearing from them, and sign off politely. Avoid phrases like "I really need this job" or "Please let me know ASAP" — they add pressure, and pressure is the opposite of what you want. **What you see:** the email might be around 80–120 words in total. That's the right length. **What happens next:** the email lands in their inbox as a calm, professional note — easy to reply to, easy to forward, easy to remember. **If it looks different:** if you don't know the next steps (some processes are slow), just say "I'm happy to provide anything else you need" — it's honest and useful. **You'll know it worked when** the email closes without begging, without bragging, and without leaving the interviewer unsure about what you want.
💬 Example: *I'm excited about the role and would love to hear how the next steps look. Thanks again, Sarah — have a lovely rest of your week.*

## Step 6 — Do a quick proofread and hit send
Read the whole email out loud once, slowly. Check the interviewer's name is spelled right, the role title matches the job ad, and there are no obvious typos. Then send. **What you see:** the final email, maybe 100 words on screen. **What happens next:** the email is on its way. Most of the work is done. **If it looks different:** if you spot a mistake after sending, don't panic — a small typo is not worth a follow-up apology. Save that energy for the next step in the process. **You'll know it worked when** you can read it back and think, "yes, that sounds like me on a good day."
💬 Example (final email): *Hi Sarah, thank you so much for taking the time to chat with me this morning about the Marketing Coordinator role. I especially enjoyed hearing how the team is planning the March launch. Our conversation about handling busy weekend rushes reminded me how much I love fast-paced, customer-facing work, and I'd be thrilled to bring that energy to Wynnum Co. I'm excited about the role and would love to hear how the next steps look. Warm regards, Jordan.*

## Common mistakes
- **Sending one identical email to everyone.** If you can't tell which interviewer it was for, they can tell you didn't write it. Always swap at least one specific detail.
- **Writing five paragraphs.** A follow-up is a thank-you card, not a second cover letter. If it scrolls on a phone, it's too long.
- **Sounding desperate or pushy.** Lines like "I really need this opportunity" or "Any update would be appreciated" add pressure. Keep the tone calm and confident.
- **Forgetting to proofread the name.** Getting the interviewer's name wrong undoes the whole "personal" effect. Double-check before you send.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** The same habit — a short, specific, timely message — works after a coffee chat, a school meeting, a meeting with a tradie, or a volunteering shift. It makes you the person people remember kindly.
- **For your work or job search:** A clean follow-up email slightly tilts the odds in your favour because most candidates don't bother, and many who do bother send something generic. Yours doesn't have to be brilliant — it just has to be real.
- **If you're just getting started:** Don't try to write the perfect email. Write a rough one, read it out loud, and send it within 24 hours. Done beats perfect every time.

## Try it now
Within the next five minutes, open your notes app and write down three things you remember from your last interview (or your last important meeting). That's the hard part done — the email writes itself from there.
